segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Saul approved of his killing. On that day a great persecution broke out against the assembly in Jerusalem, and all were scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Devout men buried Stephen and made loud lamentation over him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Saul was ravaging the assembly: going into house after house, he dragged off both men and women and handed them over to prison.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now those who had been scattered went from place to place announcing the good news of the word.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed the Messiah to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The crowds with one mind paid attention to what Philip was saying, as they listened and saw the signs he was doing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For unclean spirits, shouting with a loud voice, came out of many who had them, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So there was great joy in that city.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now a man named Simon had previously been practicing magic in the city and amazing the nation of Samaria, claiming to be someone great.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: All of them, from the least to the greatest, paid attention to him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This man is the Power of God that is called Great.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when they believed Philip as he announced the good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized he stayed close to Philip; and seeing signs and great deeds of power taking place, he was amazed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had accepted the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who went down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the Spirit had not yet fallen on any of them; they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then they laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Give me this authority too, so that anyone I lay my hands on may receive the Holy Spirit.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Peter said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “May your silver go with you to destruction, because you thought you could acquire the gift of God with money!

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: You have no part or share in this matter, for your heart is not straight before God.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So turn back from this wickedness of yours, and plead with the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and the bond of wrongdoing.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Simon answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Plead with the Lord for me yourselves, so that nothing of what you have said may come upon me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, after they had solemnly testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they started back to Jerusalem, announcing the good news to many villages of the Samaritans.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now an angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Get up and go toward the south, to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This is a wilderness road.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he got up and went. And there was an Ethiopian man, a eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasury. He had come to Jerusalem to worship,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and was now returning; sitting in his chariot, he was reading the prophet Isaiah.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Spirit said to Philip,

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “Go over and stay close to this chariot.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Philip ran up and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet, and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Do you really understand what you are reading?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “How could I, unless someone guides me?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The passage of Scripture he was reading was this:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb silent before its shearer, so he does not open his mouth.

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: In his humiliation his justice was taken away. Who will tell of his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The eunuch responded to Philip,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I beg you, about whom does the prophet say this—about himself or about someone else?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Philip opened his mouth and, beginning with this Scripture, announced to him the good news about Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As they were going along the road, they came to some water, and the eunuch said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Look, water! What prevents me from being baptized?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He ordered the chariot to stop, and both of them went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and Philip baptized him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord snatched Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, for he went on his way rejoicing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Philip found himself at Azotus, and as he traveled through he announced the good news to all the cities until he came to Caesarea.

notes.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint’s term for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses “assembly” throughout so that the reader sees it is one Greek word.

notes.phrase: announcing the good news of the word
notes.note: The verb means to bring or announce good news and was an ordinary word for public announcements. Most translations have “preaching the word” or “preaching the gospel”. The same verb recurs in verses 12, 25, 35 and 40 and is rendered with “good news” each time.

With the article and without the name Jesus, the word here is a title: the anointed king Israel expected. Samaritans had their own hope of a coming deliverer. “Christ” is kept where the word functions as part of Jesus’ name, as in verse 12; several modern translations make the same distinction.

Some manuscripts lack the article, giving “a city of Samaria”. Which city is meant is uncertain in either case. The old capital, Samaria, had been rebuilt as Sebaste and was largely Gentile, and some scholars think another town in the region is intended.

This is the same Greek word that in the plural is usually translated “Gentiles”. Here it refers to the Samaritans as a distinct ethnic and religious community. They were neither Jews nor, in Jewish eyes, simply Gentiles. Most translations have “the people of Samaria”.

notes.phrase: the Power of God that is called Great
notes.note: The wording suggests a title: Simon was acclaimed as the embodiment or representative of the supreme divine power. “The Power” could serve as a reverent way of referring to God. Exactly what the Samaritans meant by the phrase is uncertain.

The Greek word is the same one translated “Power” in verse 10 and “great” echoes the title given to Simon there, so the man hailed as the Great Power is now amazed by great deeds of power. “Miracles” is a fully acceptable rendering, but it hides this connection.

The verb carries the prophets’ call to return to God: a change of direction in mind and conduct, here explicitly “from” something. Most translations keep “repent”, which readers generally understand to include a change of life, but in modern English it centers on feeling sorry.

notes.phrase: in the gall of bitterness and the bond of wrongdoing
notes.traditional: in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity
notes.note: Peter’s language echoes the Greek Old Testament. “Gall and bitterness” describes the person who turns from God to idolatry in Deuteronomy 29:18, and “bond of wrongdoing” appears in Isaiah 58:6. Gall is bile, a byword for anything bitter or poisonous. The preposition could also mean that Simon is heading “into” this state rather than already in it.

The Greek phrase can also mean “at about noon”, which is the word’s meaning in its only other New Testament occurrence (Acts 22:6). Most translations take it as a direction, since Gaza lies southwest of Jerusalem, but a minority of scholars prefer the time reference.

The Greek says only “this is deserted” or “this is wilderness”. It may describe the road or the city of Gaza, whose old site had been destroyed and lay abandoned. It may also be either the angel’s words or the narrator’s comment; it is treated here as the narrator’s comment about the road.

“Candace” (Kandake) was not a personal name but the title of the ruling queens of the kingdom of Meroë on the upper Nile, in what is now Sudan; Greek writers called that region Ethiopia. A eunuch was barred from full membership in Israel’s assembly by Deuteronomy 23:1, though Isaiah 56:3–5 promises eunuchs a place among God’s people. The word could sometimes denote a court official without the physical sense, but Luke adds “court official” separately.

The quotation is Isaiah 53:7–8 in the Greek version, which differs from the Hebrew. The line may mean that he was denied a fair trial, or that the sentence against him was lifted. Likewise “his generation” may refer to his contemporaries, his descendants or his origin, and “taken away from the earth” may point to his death or to his exaltation.

notes.phrase: What prevents me from being baptized?
notes.note: Verse 37 is absent from the earliest and best manuscripts and is not in the Greek text translated here, so the numbering passes from 36 to 38. Some later manuscripts add: “Philip said, ‘If you believe with all your heart, you may.’ He answered, ‘I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.’” It is generally regarded as an early addition reflecting baptismal practice.
